name: Non-syndromic Vestibular Fistula

diagnosticCriteria.formalCriteriaName: Clinical Diagnostic Criteria for Non-syndromic Vestibular Fistula

criteria.description: Presence of an ectopic anal opening in the vestibule of the vagina
No associated syndromic malformations or genetic syndromes
Preserved anal sphincter muscle function on clinical examination
Radiologic confirmation of fistulous tract connecting rectum to vestibule

diagnosticCriteria.minimumForDiagnosis: Presence of ectopic anal opening in the vestibule, absence of syndromic features, and radiologic confirmation of fistula
diagnosticCriteria.notes: Diagnosis is primarily clinical supported by imaging; genetic testing is not typically indicated unless syndromic features are present.

pathognomonic.symptomName: Ectopic anal opening in the vaginal vestibule
searchTerms: ectopic anal opening in vaginal area
abnormal anal position in vaginal vestibule

pathognomonic.symptomName: Fecal discharge from the vaginal vestibule

common.notes: May be present due to altered defecation dynamics
Preserved sphincter function differentiates from other anorectal malformations

searchTerms: pain around anus during bowel movements

occasional.notes: May be present due to local irritation

rare.symptomName: Fistula tract infection with systemic symptoms
searchTerms: infected fistula with fever and symptoms
infected abnormal tract with body-wide signs

laboratory: Urinalysis may show signs of infection
Inflammatory markers may be mildly elevated if infection present
imaging: Contrast fistulography demonstrating fistulous tract from rectum to vestibule
Pelvic MRI or ultrasound to delineate anatomy and exclude associated anomalies
genetic: No known genetic mutations associated; absence of syndromic features
other: Clinical examination revealing ectopic anal opening in vaginal vestibule
Normal anal sphincter tone on digital rectal exam

distinguishingFeatures: Presence of fistula opening higher in the vagina
Often associated with other congenital anomalies
Single common channel for urinary, genital, and intestinal tracts
Usually diagnosed in neonates with multiple system involvement

redFlags: Signs of systemic infection or sepsis
Failure to thrive or poor weight gain
Presence of additional congenital anomalies suggesting syndromic association
references: Levitt MA, Peña A. Anorectal malformations. Orphanet J Rare Dis. 2007;2:33.
Holschneider AM, Hutson JM. Anorectal Malformations in Children: Embryology, Diagnosis, Surgical Treatment, Follow-up. Springer; 2006.
